name: Heron's formula
seoDesc: Heron's formula: work out side b from the perimeter and the area. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Heron's formula calculator the perimeter and the area and it returns side b. That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Heron's formula calculator work?
sections.html:
The Heron's formula calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports side b in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the perimeter and the area.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Heron's formula calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Side b=the square root of ((side a ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2) + 2 × the square root of ((side a ^ 2) × (side c ^ 2) − 4 × (area ^ 2)))
Side b=-side a − side c + perimeter

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Side a = 30 cm, Side c = 30 cm and Area = 10 cm². Working through the relationship above gives Side b = 42.4264 cm and Perimeter = 102.42641 cm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Side b = 42.4264 cm and Perimeter = 102.42641 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Side a = 30 cm and Side c = 30 cm.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Heron's formula calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the perimeter and the area — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Heron's formula calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns side b, derived from the perimeter and the area. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Heron's formula calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the perimeter and the area, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side a in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side a opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Side b = 42.4264 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Heron's formula calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
